summary: Gives best practices for writing specifications that use HTTP as a base for new application protocols. It is mainly meant to guide IETF efforts for protocols deployed on the Internet, though it may suit other situations. It is a Best Current Practice and obsoletes RFC 3205.

eli5.summary: Advice for people designing a new service on top of the web's rules.

questions: best practices for http based apis
when to use http as a substrate
how to design an http based api
should http apis use new status codes
subtitle: Best practices for specifying new application protocols that run on top of HTTP.

tldr.problem: Many applications use HTTP as a substrate, but practices that work for a single ad hoc deployment break down when an API has many implementations, uncoordinated servers and diverse clients.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists what is important about HTTP (generic semantics, links, rich features) and gives practices for specifying URLs, methods, status codes, header fields, caching, state, authentication and evolution.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 56) that obsoletes RFC 3205 and is aimed at application protocols, not at generic HTTP extensions.

today: RFC 9205 is a Best Current Practice published in June 2022. It obsoletes RFC 3205 and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Build on HTTP
sections.content:
Applications other than Web browsing often use HTTP as a substrate, a practice sometimes called creating "HTTP-based APIs", "REST APIs" or just "HTTP APIs". The RFC lists the reasons: familiarity, many available client, server and proxy implementations, ease of use, reuse of authentication and encryption, and the ability to traverse firewalls.

Many such protocols are ad hoc, built for one or a few servers and a limited set of clients. The trouble starts when an application has multiple separate implementations, runs on uncoordinated servers and is used by diverse clients. Clients and servers then evolve at different paces, so deployments with different features and versions must coexist, and extensibility has to be designed in.

RFC 9205 is written mainly to guide IETF efforts to define application protocols using HTTP, though it may apply elsewhere. It does not necessarily apply to generic HTTP extensions. It obsoletes RFC 3205.
sections.eli5: Lots of people build new services on the web because everyone already knows how it works. But a service for many people needs more careful planning than a quick one-off.

sections.title: When These Rules Apply
sections.content:
The recommendations apply when a specification defines an application that uses transport port 80 or 443, uses the URI scheme http or https, uses an ALPN protocol ID that generically identifies HTTP (such as http/1.1, h2 or h3), or makes registrations in or overall modifications to the IANA registries defined for HTTP. When they apply, all the requirements of the HTTP protocol suite are also in force.

An application can instead rely on HTTP without meeting those criteria, for example by changing how the protocol operates. That gives more freedom but loses much of HTTP's benefit, since most implementations cannot adapt easily. Such specifications MUST NOT use HTTP's URI schemes, transport ports, ALPN protocol IDs or IANA registries, and are encouraged to establish their own.
sections.eli5: If you use the web's front door, you follow the web's house rules. If you want your own rules, build your own door.

sections.title: What Is Important About HTTP
sections.content:
The first property is generic semantics. Methods, status codes and existing header fields apply to every resource, so common software such as servers, intermediaries and caches can handle a message without understanding the application. Applications MUST NOT redefine, refine or overlay the semantics of these generic elements. Application-specific meaning belongs in message content and header fields.

The RFC warns against text such as "A POST request MUST result in a 201 (Created) response." A proxy requiring authentication, a server error or a redirection can all change the status code, so clients built on that expectation are brittle.

The second is links. Assuming that a server's namespace belongs to a single application is called squatting, and it is bad practice in standards. It is RECOMMENDED that applications define and use links instead of statically defined URI components, which allows requests to move between servers without a redirection and applications to be mixed on one server.

The third is rich functionality: message framing, multiplexing in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, TLS integration, intermediaries, client authentication, content negotiation, caching, fine-grained access control through URLs, partial content and easy use from a Web browser. The RFC encourages using these features but does not require specific ones.
sections.eli5: The web's words, like "get" and "not found", mean the same everywhere, so every helper along the way understands them. Do not change what they mean, and point to places with signposts instead of claiming the whole street.

sections.title: Specifying HTTP Use, Servers, Clients and URLs
sections.content:
Specifications should use the HTTP semantics RFC, RFC 9110, as the primary reference. It is NOT RECOMMENDED to specify a minimum HTTP version, because HTTP is hop by hop and proxies, CDNs and firewalls may be in the path. A maximum version MUST NOT be specified, to preserve the protocol's ability to evolve. Examples should show both request and response with complete header sections, preferably in HTTP/1.1 format.

Server behaviour is best specified through media types, header fields and the behaviour of resources identified by link relations. For example, a spec might say that resources linked with a given relation type are Widgets, fetched in one media type and updated by PUT. Client behaviour should align with Web browsers, for example by being defined in terms of the Fetch abstraction. Applications need to say how redirects are handled, whether cookies are used, and that TLS certificates are checked as HTTP specifies.

For URLs, parts are under the control of the server's owner, so IETF specifications will not contain fixed application paths such as /app/v1. Clients can instead be given a full URL, find an entry point at a registered well-known URI, or be given a URI Template. The https scheme is RECOMMENDED for authentication, integrity and confidentiality. New URI schemes bring costs: browsers and existing clients, caches and proxies will not recognise them, and features such as cookies, caching and HSTS might not work. Applications can use ports 80 and 443 or others, but a non-default port must appear in the URL authority and has privacy and operability implications.
sections.eli5: Show full example messages, never say "you must use the newest version", and give people a front-door address to start from rather than fixing a house number for everyone.

sections.title: Methods, Status Codes and Redirects
sections.content:
Applications MUST confine themselves to registered HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT, DELETE and PATCH. New methods are rare, need IETF Review and must be generic. GET is the most useful: it allows caching and side-effect-free linking. Its processing should not change application state, because implementations retry failed GETs. For long queries the RFC says POST may be considered, at the cost of caching and linking, so supporting both is worth considering. OPTIONS has limits (it is not cacheable, is chatty and is not universally supported), so well-known URIs or linked resources are suggested instead.

For status codes, applications MUST only use registered ones and MUST NOT re-specify their semantics. Many codes come from proxies, CDNs or captive portals, not the application, and one-to-one mapping of errors to codes exhausts the finite space. So applications should make generous use of the general codes 200, 400 and 500, and put finer-grained detail in the message content or header fields. Clients should fall back to the generic n00 meaning, so 499 can be handled as 400.

Redirects differ in two ways: permanent or temporary, and whether the method may change from POST to GET.
sections.eli5: Use the standard buttons on the web's remote control. When something goes wrong, use the common "it's you" or "it's me" signals and explain details in a note.

sections.title: Header Fields, Content, Caching and State
sections.content:
New header fields are appropriate when they help intermediaries or generic HTTP software, or when values cannot go in the content. They MUST be registered, and the structured fields format is RECOMMENDED. Names should be short but specific, and an application prefix such as example-foo avoids consuming generic names. Existing fields MUST NOT be redefined. Applications should register distinct media types for each format.

Caching is one of HTTP's main benefits, providing scalability, lower latency and better reliability. Even a short freshness lifetime, such as 5 seconds, lets a response be reused. max-age is the usual way to set freshness. If caching is not wanted, no-store is the right directive, because no-cache still allows a response to be stored. Responses that vary by request header need Vary or must be uncacheable. If an application has its own validity period, it must account for the response's age.

Cookies can carry application state, but their scope must be carefully specified, since an ambient authority can be exploited. Applications MUST NOT assume anything about the relationship between separate requests on one connection, and requests have no guaranteed processing order.
sections.eli5: Let the web's memory shelves save copies so people do not keep asking the same question. Say clearly how long a copy is good, and when it should never be kept.

sections.title: Browsers, Boundaries and Security
sections.content:
Even an application not meant for Web browsers will have resources available to them, so it must consider attacks such as cross-site request forgery (CSRF) and cross-site scripting (XSS). The RFC suggests a distinct application media type with clients failing if it is not used, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, a Content-Security-Policy, a Referrer-Policy, the HttpOnly cookie flag, and avoiding compression of sensitive data.

Applications should strive to allow multiple applications on one origin, so they should not mandate particular cookie names or authentication realms. Applications exposing cross-origin data to browsers need to implement CORS. Client authentication can use HTTP authentication or TLS certificates, and Basic authentication is not suitable for sensitive information unless the channel is secure.

Server push, added in HTTP/2, has caveats: it is hop by hop, can hurt performance, varies across clients, has no browser API, and may not be supported by future HTTP versions. The 103 (Early Hints) status code is offered as an alternative. For evolution, a distinct link relation, media type or header field can introduce backwards-incompatible changes.

On privacy, the RFC notes that session information, fingerprinting and code execution can expose data, and advises specifying that clients should only emit the information they need. This document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Anything on the web can be visited by a browser, so lock the doors even if you never expected visitors. Do not spill secrets, and do not let strangers slip scripts into your pages.
